components.name: scheme
components.description: The auth-scheme Basic, matched case-insensitively, followed by one or more spaces; outside the credential span.

components.name: user-id
components.description: Text before the first colon of the user-pass; encoded inside the token, so it has no span of its own in the source.

components.name: password
components.description: Everything after the first colon of the user-pass; encoded inside the token, so it has no span of its own in the source.

claims.statement: Credentials are the auth-scheme followed by one or more spaces and a token68 (ALPHA, DIGIT, - . _ ~ + / then optional trailing = signs, no whitespace); the scheme name is matched case-insensitively.

sources.supports: credentials = auth-scheme [ 1*SP ( token68 / #auth-param ) ]; token68 = 1*( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" / "." / "_" / "~" / "+" / "/" ) *"=", excluding whitespace
For credentials, the token68 syntax is used; both scheme and parameter names are matched case-insensitively

claims.statement: The client concatenates the user-id, a single colon and the password into the user-pass, encodes it to octets and Base64-encodes it (standard alphabet) into the token carried after the scheme; the password is therefore not separately visible in the source text.

sources.supports: constructs the user-pass by concatenating the user-id, a single colon (":") character, and the password ... obtains the basic-credentials by encoding this octet sequence using Base64 (RFC 4648, Section 4)
Base 64 Encoding uses the standard alphabet and = padding

claims.statement: Only the first colon separates user-id from password; text after the first colon is part of the password, so a password may itself contain colons and a user-id may not.

sources.supports: the first colon in a user-pass string separates user-id and password from one another; text after the first colon is part of the password

claims.statement: The character encoding of the user-pass is left undefined (US-ASCII compatible); UTF-8 is only an advisory server preference (charset challenge parameter), so non-ASCII passwords arrive as encoded octets of either encoding.

sources.supports: this specification continues to leave the default encoding undefined, as long as it is compatible with US-ASCII; the 'charset' parameter is purely advisory

claims.statement: The same credentials may be carried in Proxy-Authorization, which applies to the next inbound proxy that demanded authentication and is consumed by the first such proxy; Authorization is the end-to-end carrier for the origin server.

sources.supports: Proxy-Authorization = credentials; applies only to the next inbound proxy that demanded authentication using the Proxy-Authenticate header field
for proxy authentication: Proxy-Authorization: Basic dGVzdDoxMjPCow==
A proxy forwarding a request MUST NOT modify any Authorization header fields

claims.statement: WWW-Authenticate and Proxy-Authenticate carry a challenge (scheme plus realm and optional charset), not user credentials; the realm is a free-form protection-space label compared only for equality.

sources.supports: In challenges: the scheme name is Basic; the authentication parameter 'realm' is REQUIRED ... The realm value is a free-form string that can only be compared for equality with other realms

claims.statement: Individual-user credentials identify the user even when their content stays confidential; the identity dimension of a user-id is separate from the confidentiality of the password.

sources.supports: if the server expects credentials that are specific to each individual user, the exchange of those credentials will have the effect of identifying that user even if the content within credentials remains confidential

claims.statement: Credentials apply to a protection space (realm) and to resources under the authentication scope of the authenticated URI path; this is a scope of reuse, not part of the secret.

sources.supports: the authentication scope of that request is obtained by removing all characters after the last slash of the path

claims.statement: The standard does not make Authorization a list field, so a sender must not repeat it; which of several received Authorization lines is effective, and whether a comma-joined value is a second credential, is not stated.

sources.supports: a sender MUST NOT generate multiple field lines with the same name ... unless that field's definition allows multiple field line values to be recombined as a comma-separated list; a server MUST NOT apply a request until it receives the entire request header section, since later lines might include ... deliberately misleading duplicate header fields

claims.statement: Whether the user-id inside a token is public (an identifier) or sensitive is not stated by the scheme.

sources.supports: The section describes credentials as user-id/password pairs and states nothing about whether the user-id alone is public or confidential

claims.statement: Whether a user-pass with an empty password after the colon is a valid, confidential credential is not stated.

sources.supports: The section forbids control characters in user-id and password but does not address an empty password

claims.statement: No length is stated for the token or the password.

sources.supports: The section states no length limit for user-id, password or token

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed.

openQuestions.question: Which of several Authorization (or Proxy-Authorization) field lines in one request is the effective credential, and is a comma-joined value two credentials? Header coalescing and parser policy are handed off to the product and execution repositories.
Is the user-id of a Basic credential a public identifier, personal data or part of the secret? Credential and PII populations stay separate downstream.
Does a token whose decoded password is empty carry any confidential portion?
Are tokens in base64url, unpadded or hex form, which are valid token68 but not RFC 4648 section 4 Base64, Basic credentials at all?
